label: Failure to Clearly and Expressly Advise of Right to an Independent Chemical Test
motion_heading: The Breath Test Must Be Suppressed Because {client} Was Not Properly Advised of the Right to an Independent Chemical Test

excluded_explanations.display_note: The advisement was otherwise clear, and the only complaint is that the officer explained just one type of test (e.g. blood) without mentioning alternatives. Alaska law gives the state, not the defendant, the choice of which type of independent test to offer — this alone is not a violation. See Velarde v. State, 353 P.3d 355 (Alaska App. 2015).

sentences.text: By statute, the person who administers a chemical test must clearly and expressly inform an arrestee of their right to an independent chemical test and make reasonable, good-faith efforts to assist the person in obtaining one if requested.

This requirement also rests on an independent constitutional basis: a defendant must be given clear and express notice of the right to an independent test, because due process requires an opportunity to challenge the reliability of a state-administered chemical test in the simplest and most effective way possible.
A waiver of this right is valid only if it is knowing and intelligent.
Where a breath test was administered, the remedy for a violation of this right is suppression of the test result.
Where no breath test exists to suppress, the fact-finder must instead presume that an independent test, had one been conducted, would have yielded a favorable result.

practice_notes: The state gets to choose which type of independent test to offer.
_author_notes: Pincites for Nelson (90-91) and Snyder (1278-79) on remedy_presumption_when_no_test come from earlier research notes, not a direct read of the opinions. Verify.
